title: AI-Assisted Decision Making
subtitle: Complementarity, overreliance, measuring trust, learning to defer
overview: This stage asks HAI's central empirical question: do people decide better with AI advice? It covers study design, why beating both human and AI is rare, why explanations often increase blind acceptance, measuring trust and reliance, and who should decide each case.

modules.title: A science of human-AI decisions
modules.goal: Explain how studies of AI-assisted decision making are designed, and what early studies found about accuracy, agency and bias.
modules.guide: Start with Lai et al.'s survey: each study picks a task, an AI assistance type and metrics. Lai & Tan vary how much model output is shown. The two Green & Chen papers add criminal justice and lending stakes. Key terms: 'AI-assisted decision making' (human decides after seeing AI output); 'algorithm-in-the-loop' (human decides, algorithm informs); 'risk assessment' (model scoring risk, like missing court); 'human agency' (decision reflects the person's judgment).

resources.title: Towards a Science of Human-AI Decision Making: A Survey of Empirical Studies
resources.why: Maps the field by cataloging the study design choices of over 100 empirical papers.
resources.focus: Introduction and the three main sections (tasks, assistance, metrics) with their recommendations. Skim the tables.

resources.title: On Human Predictions with Explanations and Predictions of Machine Learning Models: A Case Study on Deception Detection
resources.why: Frames assistance as a spectrum from human agency to automation; more machine influence raised accuracy, reduced agency.
resources.focus: Assistance-level spectrum and main results figure. Task: spotting deceptive hotel reviews, where humans are near chance.

resources.title: The Principles and Limits of Algorithm-in-the-Loop Decision Making
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: Proposes principles for how people should use risk assessments, then tests whether people meet them.
resources.focus: The three principles and their results, across pretrial release, lending and different risk-score presentations.

resources.title: Disparate Interactions: An Algorithm-in-the-Loop Analysis of Fairness in Risk Assessments
resources.why: Shows a fair-looking model can still yield unfair decisions, as responses to it differed by defendant race.
resources.focus: Setup and results on accuracy and on how deviations from the risk score differed by race.

quiz.q: Lai et al. organize the design choices of empirical human-AI decision-making studies into three aspects. Which set is it?
choices: Model architecture, training data, and loss function
Decision tasks, AI models and assistance elements, and evaluation metrics
Participants, incentives, and interface layout
Trust, reliance, and satisfaction
quiz.explain: The survey summarizes over 100 papers along decision tasks, AI models and AI assistance elements, and evaluation metrics, and argues the field needs common frameworks so results can build on each other.

quiz.q: Why does the Lai et al. survey argue that the field needs common frameworks for study design?
choices: Because most studies use the same task, so results are redundant
Because journals require a standard template
Because without them, varied ad hoc design choices make it hard to compare studies and produce generalizable knowledge
Because AI models change too fast for any study to matter
quiz.explain: The survey's central message is that inconsistent tasks, assistance types, and metrics make findings hard to compare; common frameworks would let researchers make rigorous choices and build on each other's work.

quiz.q: In Lai & Tan's deception-detection study, what happened when participants saw explanations alone, without the model's predicted label?
choices: Accuracy improved only slightly
Accuracy dropped sharply
Accuracy improved by more than 20%
Participants refused to make decisions
quiz.explain: Explanations alone gave a slight improvement; showing predicted labels gave a large (>20% relative) improvement. This illustrates their tradeoff: more machine influence raises performance but lowers human agency.

quiz.q: Which tradeoff does Lai & Tan's 'spectrum from full human agency to full automation' make visible?
choices: Human performance versus human agency
Speed versus cost
Model accuracy versus model size
Privacy versus transparency
quiz.explain: As assistance moves toward automation (showing labels, stating the model is accurate), human accuracy goes up but the decision reflects less of the person's own judgment. The authors find explanations can moderate this tradeoff.

quiz.q: In Green & Chen's CSCW study of risk assessments in pretrial and lending decisions, which statement matches their findings?
choices: Participants calibrated their reliance to the risk assessment's accuracy
Participants could accurately judge whether their own predictions or the model's were better
All presentation conditions eliminated bias
Only one of the proposed principles was consistently satisfied; participants could not evaluate accuracy, did not calibrate reliance, and showed bias
quiz.explain: Across conditions, only one desideratum held consistently. Participants could not evaluate their own or the model's accuracy, did not calibrate their reliance, and exhibited bias in how they used the risk assessment.

quiz.q: What do Green & Chen mean by 'disparate interactions'?
choices: The risk model has different accuracy for different races
People deviate from the risk assessment differently depending on the defendant's race, introducing bias at the human-algorithm interaction
Different participants used different interfaces
The algorithm interacts differently with judges and juries
quiz.explain: The FAT* paper shows bias can arise in how people respond to a model: participants' deviations from the risk score differed by defendant race. Fairness analysis must therefore cover the whole human-algorithm system, not just the model.

quiz.q: A city says, 'Our risk model was audited and is fair, so decisions made with it will be fair.' Which lesson from Green & Chen most directly challenges this?
choices: Models are always less accurate than people
Crowdworkers cannot be used in experiments
Fair model outputs can still produce unfair decisions because of how people interact with those outputs
Risk assessments should only be used in lending
quiz.explain: Both Green & Chen papers argue evaluations must extend beyond the model to the sociotechnical context; the human-in-the-middle can reintroduce bias.

modules.exercise: Pick one study from this module and identify two threats to external validity (e.g., crowdworkers instead of judges, no real consequences, a simplified task). For each, propose a concrete change to the design that would reduce it, and say what new cost or confound that change introduces.

modules.title: Complementarity: when is the team better?
modules.goal: Define complementary performance, explain why it is hard to achieve, and summarize evidence on when human-AI teams beat either alone.
modules.guide: Start with Bansal et al. 2021: the team must beat both human and AI alone. Then the HCOMP paper on error-boundary mental models (AAAI update paper optional). Steyvers et al. combine judgments statistically; Vaccaro et al. meta-analyze the evidence. Key terms: complementary performance (team beats both); error boundary (inputs where AI errs); backward-compatible update (no new errors where the old model succeeded); effect size (standardized difference, like Hedges' g).

resources.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
resources.authors: Bansal, Wu, Zhou, Fok, Nushi, Kamar, Ribeiro, Weld
resources.why: Reframed XAI evaluation around complementarity; explanations mostly raised acceptance of AI advice, right or wrong.
resources.focus: Introduction (critique of studies where AI alone beat the team), study design, and explanation results.

resources.title: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance
resources.authors: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Lasecki, Weld, Horvitz
resources.why: Argues a good AI teammate needs more than accuracy: people must be able to learn when it errs.
resources.focus: Definitions of error-boundary parsimony and stochasticity, and results on how they affect team performance.

resources.title: Updates in Human-AI Teams: Understanding and Addressing the Performance/Compatibility Tradeoff
resources.authors: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Weld, Lasecki, Horvitz
resources.why: Shows a more accurate model update can hurt the team by breaking what users learned about it.
resources.focus: The definition of compatibility and the proposed re-training objective; skim the dataset details.

resources.title: Bayesian modeling of human–AI complementarity
resources.why: Combines independent human and machine predictions statistically, modeling how each expresses confidence, instead of AI advising humans.
resources.focus: Significance statement, the combination model, and results on when hybrid combinations beat their parts.

resources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.why: A meta-analysis of human-AI combination experiments whose sobering average result and moderators should shape your designs.
resources.focus: Abstract, main results figures, moderators (task type; whether human or AI was better alone), and limitations.

quiz.q: According to Bansal et al. 2021, what limitation did many earlier studies showing that explanations 'improve team performance' have?
choices: They used too many participants
They never measured accuracy
They only studied image tasks
The AI alone outperformed both the human and the best team, so the human added nothing
quiz.explain: Bansal et al. note prior improvements came in settings where the AI alone beat the team; in that case the best policy is simply to automate. They test settings where AI accuracy is comparable to humans.

quiz.q: What was Bansal et al.'s main finding about explanations?
choices: Explanations greatly increased complementary performance
Explanations made people ignore the AI
Explanations increased the chance people accepted the AI's recommendation, regardless of whether it was correct
Explanations had no effect on behavior at all
quiz.explain: They observed complementary improvements from AI assistance, but explanations did not increase them; instead explanations raised acceptance of AI advice whether right or wrong, which is the opposite of appropriate trust.

quiz.q: In Bansal et al.'s HCOMP paper, what does the 'error boundary' refer to, and why does it matter?
choices: The confidence threshold above which the model is deployed; it sets cost
The region of inputs where the AI makes mistakes; if people can learn it, they know when to override
The maximum error the regulator allows
The boundary between training and test data
quiz.explain: Knowing 'when does the AI err?' lets the human accept or override appropriately. The paper shows that error boundaries that are parsimonious (simple) and non-stochastic are easier to learn.

quiz.q: Bansal et al. (AAAI 2019) show that an update which raises an AI's accuracy can lower team performance. Why?
choices: The new model is slower
The update introduces new errors on cases where users had learned to trust the old model, breaking their mental model
Users always prefer older software
The update deletes the training data
quiz.explain: An incompatible update makes errors where the old model was right, contradicting users' experience. The authors propose a training objective that penalizes such new errors to improve compatibility.

quiz.q: How does the approach in Steyvers et al.'s PNAS paper differ from the 'AI-advised human' setup in Bansal et al. 2021?
choices: It statistically combines separate human and machine predictions, modeling how each expresses confidence, instead of having a person read the AI's advice
It removes humans entirely
It uses only human crowds
It requires the human to explain the AI
quiz.explain: Steyvers et al. build hybrid human-machine combinations with a Bayesian model that accounts for differences in how humans and algorithms express confidence. This sidesteps human biases in reading advice.

quiz.q: What was the average result in Vaccaro, Almaatouq & Malone's meta-analysis of 106 experiments?
choices: Human-AI combinations performed significantly worse, on average, than the best of humans or AI alone
Human-AI combinations performed significantly better than the best of humans or AI alone
There was no measurable difference in any study
Humans alone were always best
quiz.explain: On average combinations were worse than the best single performer (Hedges' g = -0.23). Effects were heterogeneous: losses in decision tasks, larger gains in content-creation tasks.

quiz.q: Per Vaccaro et al., which condition was associated with performance gains for the human-AI combination?
choices: When the AI outperformed humans alone
When explanations were shown
When humans outperformed the AI alone
When the task was a binary decision
quiz.explain: When humans were better than the AI alone, combinations tended to gain; when the AI was better, combinations tended to lose. The authors flag publication bias and design variation as limitations.

modules.exercise: You are planning a study of an AI that helps radiologists flag fractures. Using Vaccaro et al. and Bansal et al., write down: (a) the three conditions you must include to test complementarity, (b) how you would set the AI's accuracy relative to the clinicians and why, and (c) one prediction for whether an explanation condition will help, with your reasoning.

modules.title: Overreliance and how to fight it
modules.goal: Explain why people overrely on AI advice even with explanations, and describe interventions (cognitive forcing, cost reduction, confidence display) and their tradeoffs.
modules.guide: Start with Buçinca et al.: dual-process theory and cognitive forcing. Vasconcelos et al. treat reliance as a cost-benefit choice. Zhang et al. test confidence scores; Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. show transparency can backfire. Key terms: 'overreliance' (accepting wrong AI advice); 'dual-process theory' (fast 'System 1' vs. slow 'System 2' thinking); 'cognitive forcing function' (design forcing deliberate thought); 'Need for Cognition' (enjoying effortful thinking); 'trust calibration' (trust matching actual reliability).

resources.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: Introduced cognitive forcing to HAI; the designs that cut overreliance most were the ones people liked least.
resources.focus: Dual-process motivation, the three interventions, and results on overreliance, subjective ratings, and Need for Cognition.

resources.title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
resources.authors: Vasconcelos, Jörke, Grunde-McLaughlin, Gerstenberg, Bernstein, Krishna
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: Offers a cost-benefit account of explanation use: explanations fail when they don't make verification cheaper.
resources.focus: The cost-benefit framework and Studies 1-4 summary; skim Study 5 (Cognitive Effort Discounting).

resources.title: Effect of Confidence and Explanation on Accuracy and Trust Calibration in AI-Assisted Decision Making
resources.why: Shows confidence scores improved trust calibration but not necessarily decision accuracy.
resources.focus: The two experiments' conditions and why calibrated trust alone did not improve joint accuracy.

resources.title: Manipulating and Measuring Model Interpretability
resources.authors: Poursabzi-Sangdeh, Goldstein, Hofman, Wortman Vaughan, Wallach
resources.why: Large pre-registered experiments showing 'interpretable' models do not automatically lead to better human use.
resources.focus: The 2x2 design (number of features x clear vs. black-box); results on simulating, following, catching errors.

quiz.q: Buçinca et al. explain overreliance using dual-process theory. What is their core claim?
choices: People carefully analyze every explanation but still disagree with the AI
People rarely engage analytically with each recommendation and explanation; they form general heuristics about when to follow the AI
People are unable to read explanations
Overreliance is caused by slow interfaces
quiz.explain: They argue people do not engage System 2 thinking with each AI suggestion, so simply adding explanations does not help. Cognitive forcing designs try to compel that engagement.

quiz.q: What tradeoff did Buçinca et al. find?
choices: Interventions that increased accuracy also increased overreliance
Faster interventions were more accurate
Interventions that reduced overreliance most received the least favorable subjective ratings
Explanations were preferred and reduced overreliance the most
quiz.explain: Cognitive forcing reduced overreliance compared to simple XAI, but people disliked the most effective designs. This is a practical barrier to deploying them.

quiz.q: Buçinca et al. checked for 'intervention-generated inequalities.' What did they find?
choices: Participants higher in Need for Cognition benefited more from cognitive forcing
All participants benefited equally
Participants lower in Need for Cognition benefited more
Older participants could not use the interventions
quiz.explain: On average, people who enjoy effortful thinking benefited more, suggesting cognitive motivation moderates XAI effectiveness and that interventions might widen gaps between users.

quiz.q: Vasconcelos et al. argue that overreliance is often a strategic choice. Which manipulation would their framework predict to reduce overreliance?
choices: Making the task easier to do alone and making the explanation cheaper to verify
Hiding the AI's prediction
Making explanations longer and more technical
Removing monetary bonuses for accuracy
quiz.explain: In their maze studies, costs (task and explanation difficulty) and benefits (monetary rewards) changed overreliance. Explanations that lower the cost of checking the AI make engagement worthwhile.

quiz.q: What did Zhang, Liao & Bellamy find about showing a model's confidence score?
choices: It improved both trust calibration and decision accuracy dramatically
It helped calibrate trust, but calibrated trust alone did not improve joint accuracy
It had no effect on trust
It made people distrust the AI completely
quiz.explain: Confidence helped people trust the AI more when it was confident, but improvement also depends on whether the human brings unique knowledge to complement the AI's errors. Local explanations were less helpful.

quiz.q: In Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al.'s experiments, what was a counterintuitive effect of showing a clear (transparent) model?
choices: Participants followed it much more closely
Participants could not simulate its predictions
Participants rated it as less trustworthy but used it more
Participants were less able to detect and correct the model's large mistakes, apparently due to information overload
quiz.explain: Clear models with few features were easier to simulate, but people did not follow them more closely and were worse at catching big errors. The authors stress testing over intuition.

modules.exercise: Design a cognitive forcing intervention for an LLM coding assistant that suggests bug fixes. State (1) the specific forcing mechanism, (2) the dependent variables that would show reduced overreliance without simply showing reduced reliance, and (3) how you would check for unequal benefits across users, following Buçinca et al.

modules.title: Measuring trust and reliance
modules.goal: Distinguish trust (an attitude) from reliance (a behavior), and choose appropriate self-report and behavioral measures for a human-AI study.
modules.guide: Start with Vereschak et al.'s survey of how inconsistently trust is measured. Jian et al. created the most reused trust-in-automation questionnaire. Hoffman et al. collect XAI measures. Schemmer et al. compute appropriate reliance from logs. Key terms: 'trust' (an attitude: willingness to be vulnerable); 'reliance' (following the advice); 'psychometric scale' (validated questionnaire for one construct); 'switch' or 'agreement' rate (how often people change to, or match, the AI's answer).

resources.title: How to Evaluate Trust in AI-Assisted Decision Making? A Survey of Empirical Methodologies
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: A methods survey that helps you avoid common trust-study mistakes, especially measuring trust without defining it.
resources.focus: How trust is defined and the practical guidelines section. Skim the corpus tables.

resources.title: Foundations for an Empirically Determined Scale of Trust in Automated Systems
resources.why: Source of the widely used 12-item trust-in-automation scale; its construction shows what it does and doesn't measure.
resources.focus: Collecting and clustering trust-related words, whether trust and distrust are separate, and the final item list.

resources.title: Metrics for Explainable AI: Challenges and Prospects
resources.why: A toolkit for evaluating XAI with people: explanation goodness, satisfaction, mental models, curiosity, trust and performance.
resources.focus: Skim the explanation-process model; read the satisfaction and trust-and-reliance sections. Appendices are reference.

resources.title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
resources.why: Gives a computable, two-dimensional definition of appropriate reliance, which is what most HAI studies care about.
resources.focus: The Appropriateness of Reliance (AoR) definition, computed from a 'decide first, then see advice' protocol.

quiz.q: What central problem did Vereschak et al. find in empirical studies of trust in AI-assisted decision making?
choices: Studies used too many participants
The definition of trust was usually not integrated into the experimental protocol, making findings hard to interpret and compare
Studies only used behavioral measures
All studies used the same questionnaire
quiz.explain: They found trust definitions were often missing from protocols, which can lead to overclaimed or incomparable findings. They draw on human-human trust research to propose guidelines.

quiz.q: A study measures only how often participants agree with the AI and reports it as 'trust.' What is the main conceptual problem?
choices: Agreement cannot be measured
Agreement is a behavior (reliance), which can differ from the attitude of trust
Trust can only be measured with physiological sensors
Agreement rates are always 100%
quiz.explain: Following Lee & See and the guidelines in Vereschak et al., trust is an attitude and reliance a behavior; people can rely without trusting (e.g., under time pressure) or trust without relying.

quiz.q: Jian, Bisantz & Drury investigated whether trust and distrust are separate constructs. What did they conclude?
choices: They are fully independent dimensions
Distrust cannot be measured
They behave like opposite ends of a single dimension
Only distrust matters for automation
quiz.explain: Their empirical analysis suggested trust and distrust lie on one continuum, which is why their 12-item scale mixes positively and negatively worded items into one score.

quiz.q: Hoffman et al. propose measuring several things when evaluating an XAI system. Which is NOT one of their categories?
choices: The model's training-time GPU efficiency
Explanation goodness and user satisfaction
Users' mental models / understanding
Whether trust and reliance are appropriate
quiz.explain: Their categories include explanation goodness, satisfaction, understanding (mental models), curiosity, appropriate trust and reliance, and human-XAI work system performance. Compute efficiency is not a human-centered metric.

quiz.q: Schemmer et al.'s Appropriateness of Reliance (AoR) has two dimensions. What do they capture?
choices: Speed and accuracy
Self-reported trust and self-reported distrust
Model confidence and model accuracy
Relying on the AI when it is right and relying on oneself when the AI is wrong
quiz.explain: AoR separates correctly switching to correct AI advice from correctly keeping one's own answer when the AI is wrong. Both are computed by having people decide first, then see the AI's advice.

quiz.q: Why might a researcher prefer a behavioral reliance measure plus a validated trust scale over either alone?
choices: Because attitudes and behavior can diverge, and measuring both lets you see whether an intervention changed how people feel, what they do, or both
Because scales are cheaper
Because journals forbid single measures
Because behavior can only be measured with eye tracking
quiz.explain: Vereschak et al. and Hoffman et al. both stress that trust and reliance are different. Measuring both shows whether a design changes perceptions, behavior, or their alignment.

modules.exercise: Take a study from s07m03 and rewrite its measurement plan: give a one-sentence definition of trust you will commit to, one validated self-report measure, two behavioral measures (one for overreliance and one for under-reliance), and explain when in the task each will be collected.

modules.title: Learning to defer: who should decide?
modules.goal: Explain how ML formalizes deferring cases to humans, and why it requires estimating both human and model error per case.
modules.guide: This module turns to ML formulations. Read Raghu et al. first (choosing which cases the algorithm gets), then Madras et al. (learning to defer) and Mozannar & Sontag (a consistent loss). Key terms: 'rejection learning' (abstaining, ignoring who decides next); 'learning to defer' (abstaining while modeling the human); 'triage' (allocating cases); 'surrogate loss' (easier-to-optimize objective); 'consistent' (minimizing it minimizes the true objective). Connect this to Horvitz's mixed-initiative ideas.

resources.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
resources.authors: Raghu, Blumer, Corrado, Kleinberg, Obermeyer, Mullainathan
resources.why: Reframes automation as allocating instances between algorithm and people so the whole system performs best.
resources.focus: Introduction and framework sections; skim the medical experiments for the main gain from triage.

resources.title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer
resources.why: Introduced learning to defer; modeling the downstream decision-maker improved system accuracy and fairness.
resources.focus: Rejection learning versus learning to defer, and experiments with biased or inconsistent decision-makers.

resources.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
resources.why: The standard technical treatment of learning to defer; most later work builds on its loss.
resources.focus: Problem setup and surrogate-loss intuition (treating 'defer' as an extra class). Skim the proofs.

quiz.q: What is the key argument of Raghu et al.'s 'algorithmic automation problem'?
choices: Algorithms should replace experts whenever average accuracy is higher
Humans should always review every algorithmic decision
Prediction and automation are the same task
Automation also involves deciding which instances to give the algorithm, which requires estimating both algorithmic and human error per instance
quiz.explain: They argue the debate wrongly equates prediction with automation. Triage, sending each case to whoever is likely to do better, can improve performance even on well-studied medical AI tasks.

quiz.q: How does learning to defer (Madras et al.) differ from rejection learning?
choices: It never abstains
It decides when to pass a case downstream while accounting for the downstream decision-maker's properties, including their biases
It trains the human instead of the model
It only works for regression
quiz.explain: Rejection learning abstains based on the model's own uncertainty. Learning to defer generalizes it by considering how the external decision-maker will handle deferred cases.

quiz.q: Madras et al. report that deferring models helped even with inconsistent or biased users. What did they improve?
choices: Only training speed
User satisfaction ratings
The accuracy and/or fairness of the whole system
The interpretability of the model
quiz.explain: Their experiments show learning to defer can make the combined system more accurate and less biased, because the model learns where to take over from a biased decision-maker.

quiz.q: What is the main technical contribution of Mozannar & Sontag?
choices: A consistent surrogate loss for learning a classifier and rejector, via a reduction to cost-sensitive learning that generalizes cross-entropy
A user interface for deferral
A dataset of expert decisions
A proof that deferral never helps
quiz.explain: Given samples of expert decisions, they reduce learning to defer to cost-sensitive learning and give a consistent surrogate loss, so minimizing it leads toward the optimal defer/predict policy.

quiz.q: A hospital deploys a learning-to-defer model trained on one radiologist's past decisions, but deferred cases now go to a different radiologist. Why is this a problem?
choices: The deferral policy was learned for a specific expert's strengths and weaknesses, which may not match the new expert
It is not a problem; the model is independent of the expert
The model will refuse to run
Radiologists cannot read deferred cases
quiz.explain: Both Madras et al. and Mozannar & Sontag learn deferral from the expert's decisions, so the policy reflects that expert's error profile. A new expert breaks the assumption.

quiz.q: Which HCI concern do learning-to-defer formulations usually leave out, compared with the studies in earlier modules?
choices: That humans make errors
That the human's behavior can change when they know or see the AI's output (e.g., anchoring, overreliance)
That models make errors
That some cases are harder than others
quiz.explain: These ML formulations typically model the expert as deciding independently on deferred cases. Studies like Bansal et al. and Buçinca et al. show that seeing AI output changes human decisions, a gap worth studying.

modules.exercise: Learning-to-defer papers usually assume the human's accuracy on a case is fixed. Propose a study that tests this assumption: describe how you would measure a human's accuracy on deferred cases when they (a) know the AI deferred, versus (b) do not know. What result would require changing the ML formulation?
